Dear Sion Bucker

Thank you for your email with the subject heading ‘ complaint of maladministration – defective notice, enforcement process, and loss of opportunity (Great House Farm, Llandough).

Our remit covers complaints where someone believes they've been treated unfairly or received poor service from NHS organisations or from UK government departments and their associated public organisations.

If the complaint involves public health services in Wales, this will usually fall under the remit of the Public Services Ombudsman for Wales: https://www.ombudsman.wales/

Similarly, if the complaint is related to how a solicitor or legal professional has handled a case, it is likely to fall under the jurisdiction of the Legal Ombudsman: https://www.legalombudsman.org.uk/

If your complaint is about HMCTS then you will need to complete the full complaints process and provide us with the formal response with an MP’s referral.  You can follow the link below for further information on the full complaint process:

https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/hm-courts-and-tribunals-service/about/complaints-procedure

If your concerns are primarily about judicial decisions and potential violations of his rights under the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR). As the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman (PHSO) does not have the remit to investigate judicial decisions, you could consider the following options:

  1.  Judicial Reviews and Appeals:
You will need to seek independent legal advice about the possibility of appealing the decisions or applying for a judicial review. Legal professionals can guide you on the feasibility of further legal action.
  2.  European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR):
If you believe your rights under the ECHR have been violated, you may wish to bring his case to the ECtHR. You will need to review the criteria for applying to the ECtHR at the court’s official website: https://www.echr.coe.int/.
  3.  Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC):
The EHRC provides guidance and support concerning human rights and discrimination issues in England, Scotland, and Wales. You can contact them for information or assistance: https://www.equalityhumanrights.com/en.
  4.  Citizens Advice:
For free, impartial advice, you could approach Citizens Advice, which may guide you on your next steps, including accessing pro bono legal services: https://www.citizensadvice.org.uk/.
I hope you find this information useful.

Yours Sincerely,


Anita Eastham

*Editor / Investigations Desk*

Dear Editor,

I am writing to ask your investigations team to examine what I believe is a
significant public-interest story involving one of the most influential
adverse possession cases in modern English and Welsh property law: *BP
Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] 2 EGLR 168* (also reported as *(1988) 55 P
& CR 337*).

This Court of Appeal decision continues to be cited in legal textbooks and
case law. It established that a unilateral letter from the paper title
owner granting a rent-free licence could prevent adverse possession, even
where the occupier had not expressly accepted it. The case has shaped
property law for almost forty years.

My concern is not simply with the legal judgment itself.

It is with what surrounded it.

For several years I have been investigating the history of my family's
occupation of *Great House Farm, Llandough, near Penarth*, and the events
leading to the litigation. Through hundreds of Freedom of Information
requests, archive searches, Land Registry enquiries, historical research
and correspondence with public authorities, I have uncovered what I believe
are serious inconsistencies, missing records and evidence of institutional
concealment that deserve independent scrutiny.

Among the matters that I believe warrant investigation are:

   - Whether material evidence relating to the occupation and ownership of
   Great House Farm was withheld or never presented.
   - The circumstances surrounding the registration of title by BP
   interests in 1982 despite the long-running dispute.
   - Missing or unexplained historical records across multiple public
   bodies.
   - Whether public authorities have failed to preserve records concerning
   a nationally significant legal case.
   - Whether subsequent institutions have frustrated attempts to obtain
   records through Freedom of Information legislation.
   - The wider implications if a leading legal precedent was built upon an
   incomplete or inaccurate factual record.

My investigation has revealed repeated examples of authorities either
claiming records do not exist, directing me elsewhere, or providing
documents unrelated to the requests made. Numerous archives acknowledge
gaps where relevant material would ordinarily be expected.

I have also experienced what I believe to be persistent obstruction. My
elected representatives have failed to engage despite repeated requests.
Complaints have been redirected without investigation. During my enquiries,
a court employee whom I challenged over contradictory information left
their position shortly afterwards. While I cannot infer the reason for that
departure, the wider pattern has made it exceptionally difficult to
establish an accurate historical record.

This story extends far beyond a private family dispute.

It concerns:

   - whether powerful institutions have been properly held accountable;
   - preservation of public records;
   - transparency within government;
   - the development of UK property law;
   - the treatment of ordinary families in litigation against major
   corporations;
   - and whether historical injustices can remain effectively hidden
   because records disappear over time.

The human story is equally compelling.

My family lived through decades of litigation, uncertainty and eventual
displacement. The farmhouse was ultimately demolished, ending centuries of
family association with the property. Much of my family—particularly the
women—have lived with the consequences for generations and remain reluctant
to speak publicly because of the trauma. My brother and I are now
attempting to reconstruct the historical record before more evidence
disappears.

The property itself has remarkable historical significance. Great House
Farm has connections with the historic Bute Estate, archaeological
discoveries including Roman remains, and local accounts associated with the
pioneering wireless experiments at Lavernock Point during the Marconi era.
Yet the legal battle that made national case law has largely eclipsed that
wider history.

This investigation is supported by:

   - extensive documentary evidence;
   - Land Registry correspondence;
   - Freedom of Information responses from multiple public authorities;
   - archive references from national and local repositories;
   - court documents;
   - historical maps;
   - newspaper reports;
   - and a detailed chronology spanning more than a century.

I have also recorded my testimony explaining the evidence, chronology and
impact on my family: https://youtu.be/XuArB_vYWWA?si=O7TL2i5ocU3vn5fG

I am prepared to provide your journalists with a fully indexed evidence
archive, original source documents, timelines, witness information where
available, and copies of all official correspondence.

I am *not* asking your newspaper to accept my conclusions without question.

I am asking you to investigate.

If my concerns are unfounded, they should be capable of being disproved
through proper scrutiny. If they are substantiated, they raise serious
questions about one of the UK's leading property law authorities,
institutional accountability, public record keeping and the treatment of an
ordinary family whose story has never properly been told.

This is not simply a historical dispute.

It is a story about how legal precedents are created, how power operates,
whether the historical record can be trusted, and whether ordinary citizens
can ever obtain accountability decades after the events in question.

I believe it is exactly the kind of investigation that serves the public
interest.

I would welcome the opportunity to speak with one of your investigative
journalists and provide unrestricted access to the evidence I have
assembled.

*Yours faithfully,*

*Sion Buckler*
Retired Sergeant, Royal Signals
Cyber and Electronic Warfare Professional
Life Member, Royal Signals

Dear Information Rights / Archives Team,

I am writing to request information under the Freedom of Information Act
2000 (or equivalent records access) regarding my grandfather, Mr. Williams,
who worked in the engineering department of the Cardiff Post Office /
General Post Office around 1897.

Specifically, I seek any records, personnel files, correspondence, reports,
or mentions confirming his involvement in Guglielmo Marconi’s wireless
telegraphy experiments at Lavernock Point (including erecting the 120-foot
pole and related tests to Flat Holm). This relates to contemporary
newspaper reports from May 1897.

Please provide:

   - Any personnel or service records for Mr. Williams in the Cardiff
   engineering department circa 1897.
   - Documents referencing "Mr. Williams" in connection with Marconi’s
   demonstrations.
   - Any other relevant historical files from the GPO telegraph/engineering
   teams.

My full name: Sion Buckler Address: [address redacted], Dinas Powys, Vale of
Glamorgan, [postcode redacted] Contact: [email redacted] Relationship: Great
Grandson

I am ultimately seeking any record about my great grandfather Mr Williams
of Great House Farm, Llandough, Cardiff (formerly Vale of Glamorgan). Not
to be confused with Great House Farm, Llandough, Cowbridge, Vale of
Glamorgan. And his role in the Marconi experiment. And before and after
Marconis stay with our family in our home in 1897.

I am happy to provide further identification if required. Thank you for
your assistance.

Best regards,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)

Royal Signals Cyber & Electronic Warfare Professional & Life Member

Ms Longford,

Before responding to my earlier email, please may I add the following to my
enquiry, even if you require addition time to respond due to this addition
to my enquiry;

In addition to my email of 2 July, there are a small number of further
points which I would be grateful if you could address as they arise
directly from comparing the original response with the internal review.

The original response of 11 June 2026 stated:

"Any other associated records would have been either transferred to the
Royal Commission on the Ancient & Historical Monuments of Wales for
permanent preservation, or destroyed under the Public Record Act 1958."

However, the internal review of 2 July 2026 states instead that:

"There is also no evidence that any relevant files have been transferred to
the RCAHMW."

and

"It is possible that the file was destroyed before it was ever updated on
our electronic filing system."

These appear to be materially different positions.

Accordingly, I would be grateful if you could clarify the following:

   1.

   What evidence supported the original statement that any associated
   records would have been transferred to the RCAHMW or destroyed under the
   Public Records Act 1958?
   2.

   Following the internal review, does Welsh Government now accept that
   there is no evidence that any relevant records were transferred to the
   RCAHMW?
   3.

   Does Welsh Government hold any transfer lists, accession records,
   archive schedules or other documentation recording whether records relating
   to Great House Farm were ever transferred to the RCAHMW?
   4.

   If no such documentation exists, on what evidential basis was the
   original statement regarding transfer to the RCAHMW made?
   5.

   Likewise, if there is no destruction register, disposal log or audit
   trail relating to the relevant file, on what evidential basis has
   destruction been suggested?

Finally, the original response stated as fact that Great House Farm was
visited by Cadw inspectors and did not meet the statutory listing criteria.
The internal review, however, confirms that no assessment, report or case
file has been located.

Could you therefore identify the documentary evidence upon which that
conclusion was based, or alternatively confirm whether the statement in the
original response was an inference drawn from the existence of the two
photographs rather than from any surviving assessment records.

These points are intended simply to clarify the historical record and to
reconcile what appear to be two materially different explanations contained
within the original response and the internal review.

Thank you again for your assistance, and I look forward to your response.

Yours sincerely,


Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergenant)

Royal Signals Cyber & Electronic Warfare Professional & Life Member

Dear Ms Longford,

Thank you for your response and for the time taken to clarify Cadw's
current position regarding ATISN 27021.
I note your confirmation that:

Great House Farm was inspected for statutory listing on 29 July 1988;
the two photographs formed part of that listing assessment;
the "YYY" code on the reverse of the photographs indicated that the
building did not meet the listing criteria;
no official listing file has been located; and
apart from the two photographs, no further records have been identified.
I am grateful for those clarifications.

As this request is being considered under the Environmental Information
Regulations 2004 (and, where applicable, the Freedom of Information Act
2000), and bearing in mind the EIR's presumption in favour of disclosure, I
would be grateful for one further clarification regarding the scope of the
searches undertaken.

Contemporary newspaper reports from December 1988 indicate that Cadw was
actively engaged with a number of parties during its consideration of Great
House Farm. These reports refer to:

Cadw considering emergency ("spot") listing;
discussions with the Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical
Monuments of Wales;
comments made by a Cadw spokesperson explaining why the building did not
satisfy the listing criteria; and
public statements regarding the architectural and archaeological
significance of the site.

Given those contemporary reports, could you please confirm whether the
searches undertaken for ATISN 27021 specifically included records such as:

internal memoranda;
inspector-to-management correspondence;
briefing notes;
file notes and telephone notes;
meeting records;
press office files, media briefings or press releases;
correspondence with the Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical
Monuments of Wales;
correspondence with the Welsh Office;
correspondence with the local planning authority, conservation officers or
other public bodies;
ministerial submissions or briefing papers; and
any other correspondence, whether internal or external, relating to the
consideration of Great House Farm for statutory listing.

The public interest in ensuring that all environmental information has been
identified is considerable. Great House Farm was a site with a recorded
history extending over approximately 800 years, associated with the
historic manor of Llandough, incorporating significant historic fabric
including the coach house and outbuildings, and lying within the wider
context of the Marconi wireless experiments at Lavernock. It had also been
the subject of a 1974 public petition concerning its preservation and, as
confirmed by Cadw, was sufficiently significant in 1988 to warrant
consideration for emergency ("spot") listing. These factors underline the
importance of establishing whether any additional environmental information
relating to Cadw's assessment survives.

Finally, if the official listing file and/or any associated correspondence
once existed but are no longer held, I would be grateful if you could
clarify Cadw's records management position by confirming:
whether any retention schedule applied to those records;

whether any authorised destruction took place;
whether any destruction certificate, disposal log or other records
management documentation exists;
if no such documentation exists, whether this is because no destruction
record was created or because any such record is itself no longer held.

My intention is simply to establish whether any further environmental
information relating to Cadw's consideration of Great House Farm survives
beyond the two inspection photographs already disclosed.
Thank you again for your assistance, and I look forward to your response.

Yours sincerely,

Sion Buckler

  1.  Documentary basis of the original response

The two photographs illustrate that the building was inspected for listing and ‘yyy’ reference on the reverse of the photograph was the coding at the time to signify that the building did not met the criteria to be listed.

  1.  The inspection of 29th July 1988

The photographs are dated 29/07/1988 and would have been taken as part of the listing assessment. The practice was to keep all photographs separate from the official file in a cabinet. No official file containing additional information has been located and the Records Department have indicated that the documentation from 1988 has, most likely, been destroyed.

  1.  Basis for the statement that records may have been destroyed.

No destruction record exists. An official in the Records Department provided this advice based on their experience and understanding of the records within their management.

  1.  Scope of the searches

I can confirm that the searches included all 8 categories

  1.  Welsh Government’s position.

I can confirm that the building was considered for listing, however other than the 2 photographs provided, no other records survive.

Amy

Dear Ms Longford,

Thank you for your letter of 2 July 2026 responding to the internal review of my Freedom of Information request (ATISN 27021) concerning Great House Farm, Llandough.

I appreciate the additional searches undertaken during the review and the explanation provided regarding the physical record series examined.

However, having considered both the original response of 11 June 2026 and the outcome of the internal review, I would be be grateful if you could clarify a number of points which appear to remain unresolved.

1. Documentary basis of the original response

The original response stated that Great House Farm was visited and assessed by Cadw inspectors and that the building did not satisfy the statutory listing criteria.

The internal review now confirms that no assessment, report or case file relating to that decision has been located and further states that any relevant file may have been destroyed before being entered onto the electronic records system.

Please therefore identify the documentary basis upon which the original response concluded that the property was assessed and found not to meet the listing criteria.

Specifically:

  *   Is that conclusion derived from a surviving record?
  *   If so, please identify that record.
  *   If not, please explain how that conclusion was reached.

2. The inspection of 29 July 1988

The original disclosure included two photographs dated 29 July 1988.

Please confirm:

  *   whether those photographs were taken as part of a formal listing inspection;
  *   whether they formed part of a wider inspection file;
  *   whether any inspection notes, recommendation forms, field notebooks, photographic registers or other associated records were created; and
  *   if such records once existed, whether they are now believed to have been destroyed.

3. Basis for the statement that records may have been destroyed

The review states that it is possible documentation dating from around 1988 was destroyed before being entered onto the electronic records system.

Please clarify whether that statement is based upon:

  *   documentary evidence relating specifically to Great House Farm;
  *   records management documentation such as retention schedules, destruction registers or disposal logs; or
  *   a general understanding of historic records management practices.

If no destruction records exist for the relevant file series, please confirm this.

4. Scope of the searches

Please confirm whether searches extended beyond the registered listing files to include, where appropriate:

  *   ministerial correspondence;
  *   senior officials' correspondence;
  *   legal files;
  *   inspector's working papers;
  *   site visit records;
  *   archaeological or conservation files;
  *   policy records; and
  *   correspondence with external organisations, including the Vale of Glamorgan Council, the former Welsh Office and other heritage bodies.

If any of these categories were not searched, I would be grateful if you could identify which.

5. Welsh Government's position

Finally, I would be appreciate clarification of the Welsh Government's position regarding Great House Farm.

Does the Welsh Government's position now amount to one of the following:

  *   that Great House Farm was never considered for statutory protection;
  *   that it was considered, but the records no longer survive; or
  *   that it is no longer possible to determine whether consideration took place because the relevant records are unavailable?

If none of those accurately reflects your position, I would be grateful if you could explain what the Welsh Government's position is.

These questions arise directly from the original response and the internal review and are intended to clarify the historical record rather than seek the creation of new information.

I look forward to your response.

Yours sincerely,

Sion Buckler

Dear Monitoring Officer,

I request an internal review of the Council's response to my Environmental
Information Regulations 2004 request (reference 00210772).

Thank you for the response issued on 7 July 2026. I appreciate the time
taken to consider my request and the searches undertaken. However, having
carefully reviewed the response alongside the earlier correspondence, I do
not believe my clarified request has been fully addressed, nor do I believe
the response adequately explains the scope of the searches that were
undertaken.

Clarification process
On 28 May 2026 the Council advised that the relevant service area required
clarification regarding the nature and reason for my enquiry.

I provided that clarification on 7 June 2026.
On 9 June 2026 I was informed that my clarification had been forwarded to
the Planning Department for consideration.
Given that sequence, I reasonably expected the final response to address
the full scope of my clarified request. Instead, the response appears to
have focused primarily upon identifying two planning applications and
referring me to the Planning Register.
Those applications are relevant, but they represent only one aspect of the
information requested.

Scope of my request
My request concerns environmental information relating to the historic
Great House Farm (Ty Mawr) estate, including land now forming Church View
Close and adjoining land on the north side of Leckwith Road.

The request extends from approximately 1875 onwards where records exist.
It includes, where held:

planning records;
officer reports;
committee reports and minutes;
planning consultation responses;
planning correspondence;
environmental reports;
archaeological reports;
heritage assessments;
demolition records;
redevelopment records;
engineering drawings;
highways information;
drainage and sewer records;
GIS and mapping datasets;
aerial photography;
environmental assessments;
land-related correspondence;
estate management records;
property records;
archived files;

and any other environmental information falling within Regulation 2(1) of
the Environmental Information Regulations 2004.

Matters that remain unanswered
Although the response identifies two planning applications, it does not
explain whether information was sought or considered in relation to several
parts of my request.

In particular, it does not explain whether searches were undertaken for:

archived paper planning files;
committee reports and minutes;
officer reports;
consultation responses;
supporting technical documents;
demolition records relating to Great House Farm;
archaeological reports held by the Council;
heritage assessments;
environmental assessments;
engineering reports;
highways records;
drainage records;
GIS datasets;
correspondence relating to redevelopment;
records inherited from predecessor authorities;
records transferred to Glamorgan Archives or any other repository.

Adequacy of the searches
To assist my understanding of the Council's response, I would be grateful
if the internal review could explain:

Which Council departments were asked to search.
Which electronic record systems were searched.
Which paper archives were searched.
Whether off-site archived records were searched.
Whether records inherited from predecessor authorities were searched.
Whether any GIS databases were searched.
Whether searches extended beyond the Planning Register itself.
Whether search terms or keywords were used and, if so, what they were.
Whether date restrictions were applied.
Whether any information was identified but withheld.

Information not held
Where the Council concludes that information is not held, I respectfully
request that the review explains:
which reasonable searches were undertaken before reaching that conclusion;
whether the information never existed;
whether it was transferred elsewhere;
whether it was destroyed;
if destroyed, the applicable retention schedule and date of destruction;
if transferred, the destination repository.
Information withheld

If any information has been withheld under the Environmental Information
Regulations, I request that the review identifies:
the precise Regulation relied upon;
the reasons why that exception applies;
where required, the public interest considerations;
whether partial disclosure or redaction was considered.

Planning Register
The response relies upon Regulation 6(1)(b) on the basis that planning
information is publicly available.

I would therefore appreciate clarification as to whether the online
Planning Register contains the complete planning files, including:

officer reports;
committee reports;
consultation responses;
internal memoranda;
correspondence;
amendments;
supporting plans;
technical reports;
conditions;
enforcement material (if any);
archived documents.
If it does not, I request disclosure of any remaining environmental
information held by the Council.
GIS information

The response states that my request for GIS information lacked sufficient
detail.
For the avoidance of doubt, I seek copies of any GIS datasets or historic
mapping held by the Council relating to Great House Farm/Ty Mawr, including
where available:

parcel boundaries;
planning polygons;
historic base mapping;
aerial imagery;
highway extents;
rights of way;
drainage assets;
land referencing;
scanned plans attached to GIS records.
Personal data
Separately, to the extent that any records contain my own personal data, I
request that this element of my request also be treated as a Subject Access
Request under Article 15 UK GDPR.

Closing
I have sought throughout this process to clarify and narrow my request
wherever asked to do so. My intention is simply to understand the complete
environmental and administrative record held by the Council concerning
Great House Farm/Ty Mawr.

If the Council has conducted comprehensive searches, I would be grateful if
the internal review could explain those searches in sufficient detail to
demonstrate that all reasonable steps have been taken. If further
information is held, I request that it be disclosed unless a specific
statutory exception applies.
Thank you for undertaking the internal review. I look forward to receiving
the outcome.

Regards,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sgt)
Royal Signals Cyber & Electronic Warfare Professional & Life Member
[phone redacted]

P.S. For the avoidance of doubt, where the Council holds environmental
information relating to the historic Great House Farm/Ty Mawr estate prior
to the 1989–1992 redevelopment—including records connected with the 1938
auction of the Cowbridge and Llandough Great House Farm estate, subsequent
ownership, occupation, boundary changes, estate management, landscaping,
trees, rights of way, demolition, redevelopment or associated land
management—I request that such information also be included within the
scope of this review.

In particular, if the Council holds any recorded information concerning the
removal of a commemorative tree formerly situated at or associated with
Great House Farm, including work orders, contractor instructions,
arboricultural reports, highways or grounds maintenance records,
photographs, correspondence, GIS records or file notes, I request
disclosure of those records. If no such information is held, I would be
grateful if the Council could confirm whether it has ever held such
records, whether they have been transferred or destroyed, or whether
another public authority is likely to hold them.

Finally, if, during the course of the internal review, it becomes apparent
that any part of my request has been interpreted too narrowly, I ask that
this letter be treated as further clarification rather than a new request,
so that all relevant recorded information held by the Council can be
identified and considered for disclosure under the Environmental
Information Regulations 2004.

Dear Mr Buckler

Thank you for your request for information about Great House Farm, Williams/Buckler Family, Llandough, Vale of Glamorgan and the further clarification that was received on the 7th June. Your request has been processed under the Environmental Information Regulations 2004.

The Council's Planning records have been reviewed and the Planning department has provided the following response:

In line with your clarification that was received on the 7th June, searches have been undertaken by the Council's Planning department in relation to the historic Great House Farm / Ty Mawr estate in Llandough. This includes land adjacent to and including Church View Close and the north side of Leckwith Road, with particular reference to the area identified within Land Registry title WA231076 and the timeframe indicated from 1875 onwards, where records exist.

We have been advised that the links to the planning records relating to the redevelopment of the site during the 1980s-1990s have previously been provided by colleagues in the Planning department. These records, including associated documentation, are publicly available via the Council's Planning Register and can be accessed using the relevant application reference numbers at View or Comment on a Planning Application<https://www.valeofglamorgan.gov.uk/en/living/planning_and_building_control/Planning/Planning-Applications/View-or-Comment-on-a-Planning-Application.aspx>.
This information is therefore excepted under Regulation 6(1)(b) of the Environmental Information Regulations 2004 - information already publicly available and easily accessible by other means.

Whilst planning files may contain some archaeological information, it is also noted that archaeological records for the Vale of Glamorgan are maintained by Heneb (formerly Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust). We suggest that you contact Heneb directly to access relevant records. Details on how to contact them can be found at Heneb - The Trust for Welsh Archaeology<https://heneb.org.uk/>. To the extent that the Council does not hold further archaeological reports beyond those contained within planning files, Regulation 12(4)(a) of the Environmental Information Regulations 2004 (information not held) applies.

Following searches of Planning records, no additional information has been identified within the scope of your request. You asked whether any records may have been transferred to Glamorgan Archives or otherwise. It is possible that historic material of this nature may be held externally, and you may therefore wish to contact Glamorgan Archives directly. Details on how to contact them can be found at https://glamarchives.gov.uk/contact/.

From the clarification provided, the Council has been unable to identify which specific GIS datasets are being sought. Please provide further clarification regarding this and once received, we will consider this element further.

As previously advised, the Council does not hold records relating to the legal case of BP Properties Ltd v Buckler. Neither the Vale of Glamorgan Council nor its predecessor authorities were parties to that case, which appears to have been a private legal matter. Accordingly, information relating to those proceedings is not held by the Council.

If you are dissatisfied with the handling of your request, you have the right to ask for an internal review. Internal review requests should be made within 40 working days of the date of receipt of the response to your original letter and should be addressed to:
c/o The Monitoring Officer - [email redacted]
Or by post to The Monitoring Officer, Civic Offices, Holton Road, Barry, [postcode redacted].

Please remember to quote the reference number above in any future communications.

If you are not content with the outcome of the internal review, you have the right to apply directly to the Information Commissioner for a decision.

The Information Commissioner can be contacted at:
Information Commissioner's Office - Wales
Second Floor, Churchill House
Churchill Way,
Cardiff

Dear Ms Longford,

Thank you for your letter of 2 July 2026 responding to the internal review of my Freedom of Information request (ATISN 27021) concerning Great House Farm, Llandough.

I appreciate the additional searches undertaken during the review and the explanation provided regarding the physical record series examined.

However, having considered both the original response of 11 June 2026 and the outcome of the internal review, I would be be grateful if you could clarify a number of points which appear to remain unresolved.

1. Documentary basis of the original response

The original response stated that Great House Farm was visited and assessed by Cadw inspectors and that the building did not satisfy the statutory listing criteria.

The internal review now confirms that no assessment, report or case file relating to that decision has been located and further states that any relevant file may have been destroyed before being entered onto the electronic records system.

Please therefore identify the documentary basis upon which the original response concluded that the property was assessed and found not to meet the listing criteria.

Specifically:

  *   Is that conclusion derived from a surviving record?
  *   If so, please identify that record.
  *   If not, please explain how that conclusion was reached.

2. The inspection of 29 July 1988

The original disclosure included two photographs dated 29 July 1988.

Please confirm:

  *   whether those photographs were taken as part of a formal listing inspection;
  *   whether they formed part of a wider inspection file;
  *   whether any inspection notes, recommendation forms, field notebooks, photographic registers or other associated records were created; and
  *   if such records once existed, whether they are now believed to have been destroyed.

3. Basis for the statement that records may have been destroyed

The review states that it is possible documentation dating from around 1988 was destroyed before being entered onto the electronic records system.

Please clarify whether that statement is based upon:

  *   documentary evidence relating specifically to Great House Farm;
  *   records management documentation such as retention schedules, destruction registers or disposal logs; or
  *   a general understanding of historic records management practices.

If no destruction records exist for the relevant file series, please confirm this.

4. Scope of the searches

Please confirm whether searches extended beyond the registered listing files to include, where appropriate:

  *   ministerial correspondence;
  *   senior officials' correspondence;
  *   legal files;
  *   inspector's working papers;
  *   site visit records;
  *   archaeological or conservation files;
  *   policy records; and
  *   correspondence with external organisations, including the Vale of Glamorgan Council, the former Welsh Office and other heritage bodies.

If any of these categories were not searched, I would be grateful if you could identify which.

5. Welsh Government's position

Finally, I would be appreciate clarification of the Welsh Government's position regarding Great House Farm.

Does the Welsh Government's position now amount to one of the following:

  *   that Great House Farm was never considered for statutory protection;
  *   that it was considered, but the records no longer survive; or
  *   that it is no longer possible to determine whether consideration took place because the relevant records are unavailable?

If none of those accurately reflects your position, I would be grateful if you could explain what the Welsh Government's position is.

These questions arise directly from the original response and the internal review and are intended to clarify the historical record rather than seek the creation of new information.

I look forward to your response.

Yours sincerely,

Sion Buckler

*Freedom of Information Act 2000 Request*

Sir/Madam,

I am making this request under the Freedom of Information Act 2000.

I seek all recorded information held concerning furniture, furnishings,
antiques, fixtures, heirlooms and other movable property originating
from *Great
House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough*, including any and all items we received
from *Bute Estate*, *Cardiff Castle*, *Cardiff Council. * Weather it be
museums, archives or any other public body. I know museums have artifacts
from our land in Llandough.

Specifically, I request copies of all:

   1. Inventories, catalogues and asset registers.
   2. Acquisition, disposal, loan and transfer records.
   3. Provenance files and ownership records.
   4. Photographs of items identified as originating from Great House Farm.
   5. Correspondence concerning the identification, recovery, ownership or
   location of such items.
   6. Internal reports, legal advice and memoranda relating to Great House
   Farm furniture or household effects.
   7. Correspondence mentioning the Buckler or Williams families in
   connection with these items.
   8. Records concerning any efforts by Cardiff Council or Cardiff Castle
   to trace, recover or secure items believed to have originated from Great
   House Farm.
   9. Correspondence with the Bute Estate, museums, the Department for
   Culture, Media and Sport, the Reviewing Committee on the Export of Works of
   Art and Objects of Cultural Interest (RCEWA), Arts Council England or any
   other public authority regarding objects from Great House Farm.

For context, I am allegeing that my family was unlawfully dispossessed of
Great House Farm through fraud, and that furniture and other historic
possessions belonging to the family were consequently dispersed. It's
possible the bailiffs from BP were also SAS soldiers. We are still
gathering actionable intelligence.

I appreciate that the Freedom of Information Act does not require the
authority to determine the merits of that allegation. However, it is
directly relevant to understanding why I seek the recorded information.

I am currently developing a full-scale replica of Great House Farm in
Patagonia, Argentina as a museum dedicated to preserving the history of the
house, its occupants and its contents. Should records identify surviving
items from the farm, whether held by Cardiff Council, Cardiff Castle,
museums or other public institutions, I intend to pursue their lawful
return or transfer so they may ultimately be reunited with the
reconstructed Great House Farm museum. This statement is provided solely as
context for my request and does not seek a determination under the Freedom
of Information Act.

If any information is withheld, please identify each exemption relied upon
and explain why it applies, including the outcome of any public interest
test where required.

If another public authority is more likely to hold the requested
information, I would be grateful if you would transfer the request or
advise me accordingly.

I look forward to your response within the statutory time limit.

Yours faithfully,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)

38-1-608
38-1-334

Earlier Ordnance Survey maps (pre-1950s / early 1950s) appear to consistently show the name Ty Mawr / Great House Farm in one field or parcel location.

In later editions (circa early 1970s), the label “Ty Mawr” appears to shift position between adjacent parcels, and the descriptor “Farm” appears to be applied or positioned differently than in earlier mapping.

There also appears to be a change in how the surrounding land parcels are labelled or visually grouped.

What I am seeking clarification on
Could you please advise:

Whether Ordnance Survey records show any map revision notes, resurvey information, or internal documentation explaining changes in naming or label placement for this area between approximately 1950 and 1975

resurvey work or updated field recording
cartographic generalisation or redraw practices
changes in naming conventions or feature classification

Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman,

I wish to submit a complaint of maladministration concerning the handling
of enforcement and associated administrative processes relating to my
family’s former residence and land at Great House Farm (Ty Mawr),
Llandough, Vale of Glamorgan, culminating in its demolition in December
1988.

This complaint is not a request to reopen any court judgment. It concerns
the *administrative conduct of public bodies*, including notice procedures,
enforcement execution, and heritage-related decision-making.
1. Defective and misleading notice process

I believe that formal notices issued during the relevant period were
materially defective, including being addressed to “Mrs Buckler” rather
than the legal occupier, Mary Williams.

This created a situation where the intended recipient was not properly
identified in their correct legal capacity, which I believe resulted in a *loss
of meaningful opportunity to respond, challenge, or seek suspension of
enforcement action* at the relevant time.
2. Loss of opportunity to contest enforcement

As a result of the above notice issues, I believe the family was deprived
of a genuine opportunity to take timely legal or procedural steps to
prevent or delay enforcement action, including demolition.

This constitutes, in my view, procedural unfairness in the administration
of enforcement.
3. Heritage and regulatory oversight concerns

I also believe that relevant public authorities had knowledge of the
historical and archaeological significance of the site, including Roman and
early medieval features, but failed to take adequate protective action
prior to demolition.

This raises concerns of *regulatory failure in the exercise of statutory
heritage responsibilities*.
4. Irreversible loss and harm

The outcome of these processes was the complete demolition of the property
in December 1988, resulting in:

   - irreversible loss of a long-occupied family home
   - destruction of potential historical and archaeological material
   - loss of personal and family property and records

I believe this outcome resulted from administrative failings rather than a
fair and properly informed process.
------------------------------
5. What I am asking the Ombudsman to do

I am requesting that the Ombudsman:

   1. Investigate whether there was maladministration in:
      - service of notices and identification of the correct legal occupier
      - execution of enforcement actions
      - handling of heritage-related responsibilities by relevant
      authorities
   2. Determine whether these actions caused a loss of opportunity to
   prevent or challenge demolition.
   3. Consider whether a finding of maladministration is appropriate, and
   whether this should lead to:
      - a formal apology
      - a recommendation for ex gratia compensation
      - any further remedial or restorative measures within the Ombudsman’s
      remit

------------------------------
6. Supporting material

I am in the process of obtaining further documentary evidence via Freedom
of Information requests and archival sources, including:

   - enforcement and court execution records
   - local authority and heritage body correspondence
   - any relevant ministerial communications

I will provide these as they become available.
------------------------------

I submit this complaint in good faith and seek an independent review of
administrative fairness and decision-making, not a reopening of any
judicial determination.

Regards, Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sgt)

Family records and longstanding local accounts indicate that a copy of the conveyance or land transfer associated with Daniel Thomas and the Bute Estate may at one time have been available through Cardiff's library or local studies collections. If this request would be more appropriately handled under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 or Environmental Information Regulations 2004, please treat it accordingly or transfer it internally to the relevant department.

Dear Monika,

Thank you for taking the time to search the Cardiff Central Library
collections and for your helpful reply.

I appreciate that "Williams" is far too common a surname to search
effectively without further information.

The family associated with Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough, included
Mary Doreen Williams (died 1983), her father John Williams, and later her
son, my father William Buckler and his wife, my mum; Branwen Buckler. The
property was historically known as Great House Farm or Ty Mawr and stood in
Llandough near Cardiff.

The reference to Daniel Thomas comes from historical accounts of the
quarrying and land transactions affecting the estate. My understanding is
that there was a conveyance or land exchange involving Daniel Thomas and
the Bute Estate which has been referenced in later histories of the area.
Unfortunately I do not yet have a deed reference number, which is one of
the reasons I am trying to trace the original records.

I am particularly interested in:
• Any references to Great House Farm / Ty Mawr, Llandough. • Estate records
relating to the Bute Estate and Daniel Thomas. • Local history files,
newspaper cuttings, photographs or manuscripts relating to the Williams
family of Great House Farm. • Material relating to the historic house,
farm, manor, coach house, estate, quarrying activities, or later demolition.

Thank you also for directing me to Glamorgan Archives. I have been making
enquiries there and will continue to do so.
If any estate maps, local history files, manuscript collections, newspaper
indexes, parish material, or catalogues come to mind which may contain
references to Great House Farm, I would be very grateful for any further
suggestions.

Thank you again for your assistance.

Kind regards,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)

Hi Mike,

Appreciate the reply.

I kindly request an internal review of the response provided under ATISN
27021.

I am grateful for the release of the two inspection photographs dated 29
July 1988. However, I am not satisfied that the searches undertaken were
sufficient to establish that no other relevant records are held or can be
accounted for.

The response states that Great House Farm was visited and assessed for
listing by Cadw inspectors, but that the only surviving records are two
photographs. It further states that any associated records may have been
transferred to the Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical Monuments
of Wales or destroyed under the Public Records Act 1958.

I respectfully submit that this conclusion appears difficult to reconcile
with the contemporary evidence.

Contemporary newspaper reports from December 1988 record that:

Cadw was actively considering emergency listing ("spot-listing") procedures
in relation to Great House Farm;

Cadw inspectors visited the site;
Cadw assessed the architectural and archaeological significance of the
property;
Cadw communicated a decision that the building did not warrant statutory
protection.

These activities would ordinarily be expected to generate records such as
inspection notes, recommendations, assessments, correspondence, memoranda,
listing files, briefing notes, internal communications, or decision records.

In addition, a surviving family witness who was present during the
inspection recalls that a written assessment was produced and supplied to
the family. The witness recalls that the assessment concluded that,
although the site was old, the building had undergone substantial
alteration over the centuries and was therefore not considered sufficiently
significant for listing.

This recollection appears broadly consistent with the reasoning attributed
to Cadw in contemporary press reports.
I therefore request clarification of the following:

Were searches undertaken for inspection notes, site notes, assessment
reports, recommendations, listing files, briefing papers, internal
memoranda, correspondence, and decision records relating to Great House
Farm?
Were accession records, transfer schedules, disposal schedules, or archive
catalogues searched to determine whether such records once existed?

If records were transferred to RCAHMW, please identify any transfer
references, accession numbers, file references, or other metadata recording
that transfer.
If records were destroyed, please identify the disposal authority,
retention schedule, and date of destruction.

If no written assessment, recommendation, report, or decision record ever
existed, please explain how Cadw reached and communicated conclusions
regarding the architectural and archaeological significance of the property.

I am not seeking reconsideration of the 1988 listing decision itself.
Rather, I seek clarification regarding the apparent absence of records
relating to a matter that was publicly reported at the time as being under
active consideration by Cadw and which resulted in a communicated decision.

Thank you for undertaking an internal review.

Yours faithfully,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergenant)
Cyber & Electronic Warfare Professional
Life Member of the Royal Signals

Dear Mr Buckler,

Thank you for your emails received 5-8 June.

Llandough came under Cardiff Rural District Council, 1875-1974. The plans held here have been listed and are available to search on our catalogue . There are no plans listed for Great House Farm. After this date the area come under Vale of Glamorgan Borough Council. Although some records are held for the council (catalogue available here: DCVG ) these do not include plans. No plans have been deposited by either Vale of Glamorgan Borough Council or its successor authority Vale of Glamorgan County Borough Council. We suggest that you contact them directly: planning@valeofglamorgan. gov.uk .

Correspondence received from the farm may have been reported during committee meetings: Vale of Glamorgan County Borough Council can be viewed online: CVG , and Vale of Glamorgan Borough Council: DCVG .

We do not hold any records of BP Properties Ltd or BP Pension Trust. The BP Archive (1840-2001) is held at Warwick University, and can be contacted: [email redacted] 

A catalogue to the Bute Estate records held here can be searched: DB .

Tithe maps can be searched online: Tithe Maps of Wales - Home .

Rate valuation books, 1956-1992 are here: DCVG/T/1 

There is a small Western Ground Rents Ltd Collection, consisting of three volumes, c1938-1944: D696 . However, a search of our catalogue for ‘Western Ground Rents’ will help you to locate records throughout our collections, searching for ‘Western Ground Rents AND Thomas’ may help you to identify records relating to the agreement with Daniel Thomas. A similar method can be employed to combine other search terms which will help you to identify records of relevance to your search.

If you would like to visit the Archives to view these records then details of our opening times and location can be found on our website , although please note that we are closed to the public 16-18 June to allow staff to undertake essential work on the collection. Booking is advised and if you are able to provide a list of the documents you would like to consult we will have them ready for your arrival. If you have not visited us before you will be required to register; for this we ask you bring along two forms of identification - one showing your name (e.g. driving licence, passport) and another showing your address (e.g. a recent bill or official letter).

I hope you find this information useful.

Yours sincerely,

Hannah Price
Archifydd | Archivist

LEGAL NOTICE TO RECIPIENTS:
*Take notice that this request is issued in anticipation of formal legal
proceedings and the filing of an official report regarding systemic
institutional fraud, land misconduct, and the unlawful concealment of
historic preservation data. You are under a strict legal duty to preserve
all physical and electronic records, metadata, correspondence, maps, and
erased files relating to this site. Any spoliation, deletion, or
withholding of data will be cited in subsequent court filings.*
Dear Freedom of Information Officer,
RE: Information Request under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 and the
Environmental Information Regulations 2004
I am writing to request access to historical records, internal
correspondence, planning briefs, and assessments held by your organization
regarding Great House Farm, Llandough, near Penarth/Cardiff (demolished
December 1988), and the historical occupancy of the Buckler family.
Statutory Mandate on Accessibility & Charging Fees:
I am aware that previous attempts to locate this data have resulted in
directives to visit physical archives in person or use paywalled,
commercial third-party web portals. Please be advised of the following
statutory obligations:

   1. Under EIR Regulation 8, fees cannot act as an unreasonable barrier or
   deterrent to access. Because my family was historically displaced from this
   site and I am executing this request remotely, forcing physical attendance
   or demanding payment constitutes an unlawful obstacle.
   2. Public authorities are required to supply information in the format
   requested. I require all documents to be delivered digitally via email
   attachment or secure electronic download link, free of charge, as
   specified by the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) guidelines for
   data already held electronically.

Please provide all recorded information matching the following points:
1. Tenant/Ownership Identification and the 1880 Report

   - Any documents, archival notes, or registry indexes citing the
William/ Buckler
   family line (who occupied and farmed the house across four generations).
   - Clarification on whether my family members were formally cited as the
   legal owners, long-term tenants, or registered reporters of the 1880
   discovery under the dining room floor.
   - Any explicit records indicating gaps, deleted metadata, or missing
   volumes in your authority’s archive concerning the tenancy, land-dispute
   maps, or agricultural heritage of Great House Farm between 1950 and 1989.

2. Statutory Protection and Cadw’s Assessments

   - Given that the site's extreme archaeological value (a
   1st-to-4th-century Roman precursor villa and a massive early medieval
   monastic settlement) was verified by rescue operations as early as 1979,
   what are the recorded reasons why Cadw failed to place a statutory
   Schedule or Protection Order on the standing fabric of Great House Farm
   before its demolition?
   - All internal correspondence, risk assessments, or ministerial briefs
   evaluating the preservation value of the sub-medieval direct-entry
   farmhouse core before it was levelled.

3. Planning Approvals and Local Authority Governance

   - All minutes, planning committee files, and consultation responses from
   the local authority that granted planning permission and housing
   development rights on this specific acreage.
   - Direct information explaining how the council approved planning
   permission for a private housing development in light of the documented
   historical evidence surrounding the immediate parish boundary.

4. Institutional Concealment and Historical "Ignorance"

   - Records showing exactly where and at what stage of the planning
   process this archaeological evidence should have been brought up
but was not,
   which ultimately allowed developers and public bodies to claim they were
   unaware of the land's deep significance until after the farmhouse was
   destroyed and housing development began.
   - Any environmental impact assessments, historic environment register
   (HER) lookups, or developer briefs filed between 1980 and 1990 regarding
   the footprint of Great House Farm.

If any part of this request is refused under the guise of commercial
sensitivity or archival limitations, you are required by law to state the
exact statutory exemption applied and provide a formal internal review
pathway.
I expect your response within the statutory 20-working-day timeframe.
Kind regards,
*Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)*
*[address redacted], Dinas Powys, Vale of Glamorgan*

Good afternoon,

Thank you for your enquiry. As noted in my email of 26 November last, while we cannot advise you on a legal case or undertake a review of historical decisions, we do hold information and archives related to Great House Farm, Llandough.

The site entry and description for the site in the National Monuments Record of Wales can be seen online on Coflein, here: https://coflein.gov.uk/en/site/20182.

We hold 14 archives related to the site, a list of which can be seen here: https://coflein.gov.uk/en/site/20182/archives?size=25. These archives can be viewed in our Search Room, located in the National Library of Wales, which is open Tuesday through Thursday, 9:30-16:30. If you would like to view the material in person, I would advise arranging with us beforehand so that we can prepare the material ahead of your visit. Some of the material is on microfiche and as we do not have a microfiche reader in the Search Room, we will need to liaise with the National Library Reading Room staff to try to negotiate the use of their machines ahead of your visit. However, I have located an electronic copy of Archive Number 6524751, which can be accessed here: https://www.walesher1974.org/her/app/php/herumd.php?group=GGAT&level=3&docid=301361628

While it is possible to order scans of material using the attached order form, we may be unable to provide research-quality scans or photographs of some of the material, such as the material on microfiche, which would require high-resolution scanning at a cost of £20 per scan.
